What Is Asphalt Made Of?

materials 14 Aug 2026

Sentence32 words · 0.2 min

Asphalt pavement is about 95% crushed rock by weight, glued together by a 5% film of bitumen — the black, tar-like residue left at the bottom of an oil refinery’s distillation column.

The road you drive on is mostly stone. Asphalt concrete is a carefully sized skeleton of crushed rock, gravel, sand and dust — about 95% of the mix by weight — coated in a thin film of bitumen, the heaviest fraction of crude oil, which is the other 5%. The rock carries the load; the bitumen only holds it in place and keeps water out. What makes the material interesting is that the glue is not a solid. Bitumen is viscoelastic: on a hot afternoon it flows, and on a January night it behaves like glass. Almost every road failure is a story about that binder.

Start with the rock, because that is what asphalt mostly is. A mix design specifies a gradation: what fraction of the aggregate passes through each sieve, from 25 mm stones down to dust finer than 0.075 mm. The goal is a structure where large stones bear against large stones, with smaller particles filling the gaps well enough to be stable but not so completely that no room is left. Engineers deliberately leave roughly 4% air voids in a finished pavement. Too few voids and the mix has nowhere to expand into on a hot day, so it shoves sideways under a truck tyre. Too many and water and oxygen get inside, and the pavement ages from within.

Then the glue. Bitumen is what remains after crude oil has given up its gasoline, kerosene, diesel and lubricating oils — the bottoms of the vacuum distillation tower. Chemically it is a colloid: large, polar, sooty molecules called asphaltenes suspended in an oily medium of saturates, aromatics and resins. Change that balance and you change the road. Refineries and suppliers grade binders by the temperatures they must survive: a PG 64-22 binder is certified to resist rutting up to a 64 °C pavement temperature and cracking down to −22 °C. Polymers, usually styrene-butadiene-styrene rubber, stretch that window at both ends for highways and airport runways.

Finally, heat, which is the whole manufacturing process. At a hot-mix plant the aggregate is dried and heated to roughly 150 °C, the binder is pumped in at a similar temperature, and for a few minutes the mixture is fluid enough to haul, spread and compact. Then it cools, and cooling is the only “setting” that occurs — no chemical curing, no hydration like concrete. This is why asphalt is the most recycled material by mass in many countries: old pavement is simply milled up, reheated, and made fluid again. Reclaimed asphalt pavement routinely makes up 20–30% of a new mix, and some plants go far higher.

It is a rock structure with a very thin coat of glue.

Take a core out of a road and look at the cut face. You will see stones — angular, crushed, of many sizes — packed against one another, with black film in the gaps between them. By weight, that stone is about 95% of what you are holding. The bitumen film averages perhaps 8–10 micrometres thick. The road is not a slab of tar with pebbles in it; it is a pile of rock that has been persuaded to hold hands.

The rock is sized, not just dug up.

Aggregate arrives from a quarry, is crushed to make angular faces (rounded river gravel rolls past its neighbours instead of locking against them), and is separated into sieve fractions that are then recombined to a designed gradation curve. Dense-graded mixes fill nearly every gap and make a smooth, watertight wearing course. Open-graded friction courses deliberately leave large connected voids so that rain drains sideways through the surface instead of sitting on it as spray. Stone-mastic asphalt uses a gap gradation — lots of big stone, little middle-sized material — plus cellulose fibre to stop the rich binder mortar from draining out; it is heavy, expensive and extremely tough under studded tyres.

The binder is a temperature-dependent liquid pretending to be a solid.

Bitumen has no melting point. It simply gets less viscous as it warms, across an enormous range: it is stiffer than steel in behaviour at −30 °C and pourable at 150 °C. Engineers characterise this with the Performance Grade system. The first number is the highest average seven-day pavement temperature the binder can handle without rutting; the second is the lowest temperature it can reach before it cracks from thermal contraction. A binder is not chosen for a road so much as for a climate.

Everything that goes wrong is a binder story.

Rutting is the mix shoving sideways under load, usually because the binder is too soft for the summer or because the aggregate skeleton lacks angular interlock. Fatigue cracking — the alligator pattern in a wheel path — is the pavement flexing over a weak base, thousands of times, until the bottom of the layer tears. Transverse cracks, evenly spaced across the road, are the pavement shrinking on the coldest night of the year. And underneath all of these sits oxidative ageing: the binder slowly reacts with air, loses its lighter oily fractions, and stiffens. An old road is a brittle road, which is why the surface eventually ravels away, stone by stone.

It is also the most recyclable pavement there is.

Because the material only cools rather than cures, a road at the end of its life is not waste; it is aggregate that already carries binder. Milling machines grind up the old surface, and the millings go straight back into a new mix, with a small dose of softer virgin binder to rejuvenate the aged film. Warm-mix additives and foaming now let plants work 20–40 °C cooler, cutting fuel and fumes. The road you drove on this morning has probably already been part of two or three earlier roads.

A material named after a lake

Long before refineries, asphalt came out of the ground. Natural bitumen seeps to the surface wherever heavy crude sits under the right geology: the tar pits at Rancho La Brea, the bituminous sands of Alberta, and above all Pitch Lake in Trinidad, a 40-hectare pool of asphalt that has been mined continuously since the 1860s and simply refills itself. Mesopotamian builders used bitumen as mortar and waterproofing five thousand years ago. Egyptian embalmers used it too, and the confusion of that black substance with the Persian word mumiya eventually gave English the word “mummy”.

The modern road is younger than most people assume. Nineteenth-century engineers, notably John Loudon McAdam, worked out that a well-drained bed of graded, angular broken stone could carry heavy loads without a masonry foundation. Those macadam roads worked beautifully for iron-shod wheels and horribly for pneumatic tyres, which sucked the fine binding dust out of the surface and turned every dry summer into a dust storm. The fix was to spray the surface with a black liquid to hold the dust down. First came coal tar, a by-product of town gas works — hence “tarmacadam” and “tarmac”. Coal tar is chemically unrelated to bitumen, far more carcinogenic, and has been almost entirely abandoned for road work, though the name it left behind still causes confusion. When petroleum refining scaled up in the early twentieth century, refinery bitumen replaced tar, and the modern hot-mix asphalt plant was born.

The vocabulary never quite settled. In American usage, “asphalt” means the binder and, loosely, the pavement. In British usage the binder is “bitumen” and “asphalt” is the mixture. Australians say “bitumen” for the whole road. They are all talking about the same black stuff.

What is actually in the barrel

Crude oil entering a refinery is separated by boiling point. The lightest fractions leave the top of the atmospheric tower as gases and gasoline; then kerosene, then diesel. What will not boil at atmospheric pressure goes to a vacuum tower, where reduced pressure allows more distillation without cracking the molecules by heat. What refuses to boil even there — the vacuum residue — is bitumen. It is the accumulated remainder of everything in the original crude that is too large, too heavy and too aromatic to have escaped earlier.

Chemists describe this residue with the SARA fractions: saturates, aromatics, resins and asphaltenes. The asphaltenes are the heart of the matter — large, polar, polycyclic aromatic clusters, essentially soot that has not yet been burned, carrying nitrogen, sulphur, oxygen, and traces of nickel and vanadium inherited from the marine organisms the oil once was. Asphaltenes do not dissolve in the oily maltene phase around them; they disperse in it, stabilised by the resins that coat them, in a colloid. Stiffness comes from the asphaltene content and the way those clusters associate. Flexibility comes from the maltenes.

Ageing is the slow destruction of that balance. Oxygen attacks the aromatic and resin fractions, converting them into more polar species that behave like additional asphaltenes; volatile light ends evaporate during hot mixing and slowly thereafter. The colloid becomes richer in the stiff phase and poorer in the soft one. This is not corrosion of the road in any dramatic sense. It is a pavement gradually becoming a different, more brittle material than the one that was laid.

Designing a mix

A mix design is an experiment in packing and proportion. The designer selects aggregate sources and blends their sieve fractions to hit a target gradation, then produces trial specimens at several binder contents, compacts them in a gyratory compactor that imitates the kneading of a roller and years of traffic, and measures the resulting density. The chosen binder content is the one that lands the compacted specimen at roughly 4% air voids with adequate voids in the mineral aggregate — enough space between stones to hold a durable film of binder without letting the mix become unstable.

Too little binder and the film is thin, the mix is dry and permeable, and the surface ravels. Too much and there is not enough void space; on a hot day the expanding binder has nowhere to go, the mix loses internal friction and the pavement ruts or bleeds shiny black to the surface. The window between those failures is only about half a percent of binder by weight. Asphalt production is a business of narrow tolerances carried out by very large machines.

Additives widen the window. SBS polymer forms an elastic network through the binder, raising high-temperature stiffness while preserving low-temperature flexibility — the single most common upgrade for heavy-duty pavements. Crumb rubber from scrap tyres does some of nickel and vanadium inherited from the marine organisms the oil onceortars in place. Warm-mix chemicals or foamed water reduce viscosity at lower temperatures, letting a plant run 20–40 °C cooler with real savings in fuel, emissions and worker exposure.

Laying it, and what happens next

At the plant, aggregate is dried in a rotating drum, dust is captured and returned, binder is metered in hot, and the mix is stored briefly in an insulated silo. Trucks carry it under tarpaulins to the paver, which spreads it in a mat of controlled thickness whil

Beneath the visible surface there is usually a structure of layers — a thin wearing course chosen for friction and noise, a binder course, a base course, all resting on a granular base and subgrade. Load from a tyre spreads through this stack in a cone, so the surface handles high contact stress and the deeper layers handle diffuse pressure. The most expensive material sits where it does the most good, at the top. Perpetual pavement designs go further: a very durable, flexible base layer that never fatigues, so that maintenance forever after only involves milling and replacing the top few centimetres.

That maintenance loop is why asphalt survives environmental scrutiny better than its appearance suggests. The material is thermoplastic. It is reheatable, remixable and, in principle, endlessly reusable — reclaimed asphalt pavement is recycled at higher rates than paper, glass or aluminium in several countries. The open questions are the ones you cannot see from the car: the energy burned to dry and heat aggregate, the fossil origin of the binder itself, and the heat that a black surface returns to a city on a summer evening. Research runs toward bio-binders from lignin and vegetable pitch, toward mixes laid at ever lower temperatures, and toward lighter-coloured surfaces that keep neighbourhoods cooler.

For now the recipe stays roughly the same as it was a century ago: crush the right rock, size it carefully, warm it up, and hold it together with the last thing left in the barrel.
